claim: A runtime failure detector for robot policies trained only on whole-episode success or failure labels can learn to raise its alarm at or before the moment a failure actually begins, rather than after the failure has played out, even though it is never told when any failure began. Supported only if, measured against failure-onset times annotated independently of the detector (and checked against human raters), the detector's mean alarm time over correctly detected failures is no later than the annotated onset in every policy and seen/unseen task split tested, whereas the strongest prior classifier trained on the same labels alarms late in at least one; and if across the full range of false-alarm settings it gives a better accuracy-versus-detection-time trade-off than the alternatives.

experiments: Collect rollouts and fix the splits. Setup: run released fine-tuned checkpoints of an autoregressive policy (OpenVLA) and a flow-matching policy (pi0) on the ten long-horizon LIBERO-10 tasks, and a second flow-matching policy (pi0.5) on ten VLABench tasks. In each benchmark hold out three of the ten tasks as unseen, with a different random partition for each of three seeds. Per benchmark: 210 training rollouts, 35 held-out successful rollouts for calibration, 105 evaluation rollouts on seen tasks and 150 on unseen tasks. Label each rollout only as success or failure. Base success rates are 51.0% (OpenVLA), 84.2% (pi0) and 40.3% (pi0.5). Extract a per-step embedding from the policy's action token or action head, averaged across layers for the autoregressive model and taken before the velocity head at the last denoising step for the flow models, then average over non-overlapping windows.

Fix how an alarm is decided and scored, for every method alike. Setup: turn per-step failure scores into alarms with a time-varying threshold built by functional conformal prediction from held-out successful episodes, which bounds the trajectory-level false-alarm rate on successful runs at alpha. Count a failure episode as detected if an alarm fires at any step. Report balanced accuracy, accuracy weighted by class frequency, and time-weighted accuracy, which discounts each true detection by how late in the episode it fires, averaged over alpha in {0.15, 0.20, 0.25} and three seeds. Tune all hyperparameters, for the new detector and for every baseline, only on seen tasks, then apply them unchanged to unseen tasks. For unseen tasks the calibration set comes from seen tasks, since unseen tasks are not available at calibration time.

Obtain failure-onset times independently of the detector and check them against people. Setup: give a multimodal model (GPT-5.2) each recorded failed video offline, with a strict definition of failure start as the earliest frame where an irreversible mistake appears or behaviour becomes clearly unrecoverable, and ask for one frame index with visual evidence. Use these times only for analysis, never for training or the main metrics. Validate with four PhD-level ML researchers who each mark agree or disagree, allowing small offsets, on 76 failed rollouts. Result: 90.7% agreement over 304 ratings, unanimous agreement on 75.0% of rollouts, and no rollout unanimously rejected.

Measure how early alarms fire relative to the annotated onset. Setup: on LIBERO-10 with OpenVLA and pi0, seen and unseen tasks, compute over correctly detected failure episodes the mean of (annotated onset minus first alarm) divided by episode length, so positive means early; average over alpha in {0.15, 0.20, 0.25} and three seeds; compare with both SAFE variants. Result: the new detector is early in all four settings (+0.042, +0.019, +0.078, +0.052) while also being most accurate. SAFE-MLP alarms late in three of four (-0.057, -0.272, -0.052, with +0.121 on pi0 seen), and SAFE-LSTM is late on OpenVLA unseen (-0.147) with lower accuracy.

Trace the whole accuracy-timeliness trade-off rather than one operating point. Setup: sweep alpha from 0.01 to 1.0 in steps of 0.01 on unseen LIBERO-10 tasks for OpenVLA and pi0 and plot, for each method, balanced accuracy against mean normalised detection time, marking the mean annotated onset. Result: the new detector's curve lies closest to the top-left (earlier and more accurate) of all methods for both policies.

Check that the detector's own sharpest score rise lands where failures actually begin. Setup: on LIBERO-10, compare three per-episode times, all normalised by length: the step of peak failure score, the step of the largest single-step score increase (which no loss targets directly) and the annotated onset; then train with each as the anchor for the before/after separation term. Result: the largest-increase step sits at 0.417 against an annotated 0.401 for OpenVLA and 0.470 against 0.478 for pi0, while the peak step lags at 0.508 and 0.546. Anchoring on the largest-increase step matches the annotated-onset anchor (OpenVLA unseen balanced accuracy 0.834 vs 0.836), while anchoring on the peak step lowers both accuracy and timeliness.
